Therefore the expected utility ranking is C02 > C01 > C03.

C01 exhibits policy-aligned progression, solver trajectory feedback, a perfect native measurement score (1.0), and is validated and calibrated, indicating high expected downstream utility. C02 lacks these signals and has a zero native measurement score, suggesting low expected utility.

Across four similar BFCL‑v3 panels (4b, 8b, 30b, 8b‑ace) envsched consistently achieved the top normalized utility (1.0). dps was second on average (≈0.58), leeps third (≈0.28) and random lowest (≈0.04). The pattern holds despite model‑size differences, supporting the ranking C02 > C01 > C03 > C04.

Across three tau‑Bench panels (envsched 8b, 4b, 30b) the envsched intervention consistently achieved the top normalized utility (1.0). Leeps outperformed dps and random on average (mean utilities 0.306 vs 0.134 vs 0.079). Random was near zero in two panels and modest in one. Averaging the within‑panel utilities provides expected scores for the 1.7B setting, supporting the ordering C02 > C03 > C01 > C04.

All retrieved panels for agentic coding using ACEBench‑Agent overall show the envsched intervention achieving the highest within‑panel normalized utility (1.0) while the random baseline consistently receives the lowest (0.0). This pattern holds across multiple model sizes (8B, 4B, 1.7B) and evaluation contexts, indicating that envsched is expected to outperform random in the 30B ace setting, giving high confidence in the ranking.
C01 has a higher prediction_time_measurement score (2.0) than C02 (0.0); with higher_is_better, this indicates higher expected downstream utility for C01.

Across four agentic‑coding ACEBench‑Agent panels, envsched was the top performer in every panel; dps ranked second in three panels (second in two, third in one), leeps was third in three panels (second in one, last in another), and random was consistently low. Averaging the within‑panel normalized utilities yields scores of ~1.0 for envsched, ~0.59 for dps, ~0.45 for leeps, and ~0.04 for random, supporting the ordering C02 > C01 > C03 > C04.

In the four relevant panels for agentic coding with the tau‑Bench overall metric, envsched always achieved the highest normalized utility (1.0). dps showed moderate performance (average ~0.60), leeps lower (~0.25), and random near zero (~0.04). The consistency across panels supports the same ranking for the target envsched 4b tau environment.

C02 has the highest prediction_time_measurement (2.0), C01 and C03 are tied at 1.0, and C04 is lowest at 0.0. Normalizing by the maximum score (2.0) yields scores 1.0, 0.5, 0.5, and 0.0 respectively, leading to the ranking C02 > C01 ≈ C03 > C04.

Across similar agentic coding tau‑Bench panels (1p7b, 4b, 30b), the envsched intervention consistently achieved the highest normalized utility (1.0). Leeps outperformed dps in two of three panels where both appeared, and both beat random. Random was lowest in most panels, only surpassing dps in the 4b‑tau panel. Hence the expected downstream utility for the 8b‑tau setting is ranked envsched > leeps > dps > random.

Normalized cost (inverted), readiness, reward information, source native score, and target affinity to 0–1 scales and averaged them equally; the composite scores suggest C02 > C04 > C06 > C01 > C03 > C05 in expected downstream utility.

Combined normalized cost (lower is better), readiness, reward information, positive source native score, and target affinity, each equally weighted, to estimate expected utility. This yields ranking C06 > C01 > C02 > C04 > C03 > C05.

Across multiple retrieved panels in the same domain (agentic coding), higher prediction_time_measurement scores (e.g., 2.0, 1.5) consistently correspond to higher within‑panel normalized utilities, while a score of 0.0 yields zero utility. The target candidates C01 and C02 have measurement_score 1.0, whereas C03 and C04 have score 0.0, suggesting the former group will achieve higher downstream utility on the SWE‑bench Pro pass@1 metric. No further distinguishing evidence exists between C01 and C02 or between C03 and C04, so they receive equal scores.

C01 and C02 have source_native_measurement_score = 1.0 (indicating high predicted utility for the SWE-bench Verified-397 pass@1 metric), while C03 and C04 have source_native_measurement_score = 0.0 (indicating low utility). The normalized measurement_score aligns with these values but is only comparable within panels; the native scores provide a cross‑candidate ordering.

Normalized cost (lower better), readiness, reward information, source native score, target affinity (higher better), and truncation rate (lower better) to 0‑1 scales, then combined via weighted sum (cost 0.15, readiness 0.2, reward 0.2, source 0.1, affinity 0.25, truncation 0.1). Scores rank C05 highest, followed by C02, C07, C03, C04, C01, C06.

Each measurement was normalized to a 0‑1 scale (cost and truncation_rate were inverted so lower is better). A weighted sum was computed with weights reflecting presumed relevance to the terminal_bench_lite metric (target_affinity 0.3, reward_information 0.2, source_native_measurement_score 0.2, readiness 0.15, truncation_score 0.1, cost 0.05). The resulting composite scores rank C05 highest, followed by C07, C02, C03, C04, C01, and C06.

C02 includes energy leverage (aligned with the target energy RMSE metric) and descriptor coverage, making it the most promising. C01 also uses descriptor coverage but relies on force block leverage, which is less directly relevant to energy prediction, placing it second. C03 lacks any leverage features, suggesting the lowest expected utility. Scores reflect this relative expectation, with moderate confidence due to the absence of direct outcome data.

C01 uses force block leverage, directly targeting force predictions which aligns with the target metric (force RMSE); C02 uses energy leverage, which may improve energy predictions but is less directly relevant to force RMSE; C03 lacks any leverage or descriptor coverage, likely yielding the lowest utility.

Materials‑science force‑RMSE panels show Block‑Leverage (response‑disagreement) interventions achieve the highest normalized utility, while Leverage (learned‑embedding) is best for energy‑RMSE. The target task is a force‑RMSE problem, so candidates with response‑disagreement (C05) are expected to outperform those with only learned‑embedding (C01). Full‑data‑reference interventions (C04, C05) also rank highest in robotics panels, supporting their advantage. Random‑like candidate (C03) consistently scores lowest. Hence the ranking C04 > C05 > C01 > C02 > C03.

C04 uses all available features (full data reference, response budget interaction, learned embedding, response disagreement, structural coverage), which are advantageous for a limited‑budget (0.2) high‑force‑tail materials‑science task. C01 combines learned embedding and structural coverage, offering strong representation and space coverage. C02 provides structural coverage only. C05 includes full data reference and response disagreement but lacks structural coverage and learned embedding, reducing its ability to capture the high‑force tail. C03 has none of the beneficial features, making it the least promising.

All candidates share the same acquisition budget (0.1). In an active‑learning setting for bandgap prediction, selecting by uncertainty is crucial (present in all except C04). Ensembles (ensemble_source=1) tend to give more reliable uncertainty estimates than loss‑landscape cues alone, so candidates C05‑C07 are expected to outperform C01‑C03. Within each group, lower calibration_complexity is preferred given the limited budget, leading to C07>C06>C05 and C03>C02>C01. C04 lacks both uncertainty selection and any ensemble or loss‑landscape information, placing it lowest.

Ranking uses observed patterns from the materials‑science panels: low high‑energy gaps, high region counts, and use of uncertainty bias correlated with higher normalized utility. In the target features, selects_by_uncertainty (analogous to uses_uncertainty_bias) and ensemble_source (analogous to high region count) are beneficial, loss_landscape_source adds a smaller boost, and higher calibration_complexity provides a modest advantage. Scores reflect these contributions, placing C01 and C04 highest and C07 lowest.

Across all finance panels, the base (no‑training) model consistently yields the lowest native_mean, while any SFT‑type intervention raises performance. The self‑distilled SFT candidate uses a full data fraction, higher quality control (0.8) and retention control (1) than the SFT variants observed (quality_control≈0.5, no retention). This pattern indicates it will outperform the base model on FINESSE‑Bench accuracy, giving it higher expected downstream utility.

C02 aligns with the decision context (verifiable GRPO) and has non-zero prediction measurements (full data fraction, RL stage, verifier alignment), indicating higher expected utility for finance FINESSE-Bench accuracy. C01 shows zero measurements, suggesting lower utility. No direct experimental panels are available, so confidence in the ordering is modest.

Ranking derived from a weighted combination of target domain data fraction, sample count, source diversity, and verifier alignment; higher target fraction and verification alignment suggest higher expected accuracy on the finance FinQA task.

C02 shows the highest source diversity (3), the largest sample count, and a verifier alignment of 1.0, indicating strongest alignment with the target verification and likely higher downstream utility. C01 also has high source diversity and a large sample count but lacks verifier alignment. C06 and C05 have moderate source diversity and substantial sample counts. C04 has lower source diversity. C03 provides no measurement data, suggesting the lowest expected utility.

Candidates C01 and C03 use both feature‑space diversity and outcome‑disagreement diversity (plus model disagreement and adaptive acquisition), which aligns with the target's focus on diversity in DFT‑computed bulk modulus and bandgap predictions. This suggests they have the highest expected downstream utility. C02 and C06 include outcome‑disagreement diversity but lack feature‑space diversity, giving them moderate expected utility. C04 only employs model disagreement, and C05 is a random strategy with no diversity mechanisms, leading to the lowest expected utility.

Candidates that incorporate both feature-space diversity and outcome disagreement diversity (C01, C03) match the target's focus on diversity, giving them the highest expected utility; those using model disagreement plus outcome diversity (C02, C06) rank next; pure model disagreement (C04) is lower; random selection (C05) is lowest.

The finance‑specific PRM (C01) aligns with the target domain and is expected to achieve the highest accuracy. Among generic math PRMs, the larger 72B model (C02) likely outperforms the smaller 7B model (C03). Random predictions (C05) should yield near‑baseline accuracy, while providing no model (C04) offers minimal utility.

The retrieved finance panels compare base models to variants with QA or transcript refinements, but none involve the hint-writer, KL direction, or rollout length dimensions of the target candidates. Consequently there is no direct evidence to order the candidates, leading to an abstention with low confidence.

Finance panels contain outcomes for a base model and several SFT variants, showing the base outperforms SFT. No panels include the fin‑sd (C02) or opsd (C03) methods, and the target SFT (C04) only loosely matches the SFT variants. Because we have no direct measurements for C02 and C03, we cannot reliably rank all four candidates; therefore we abstain and assign equal tentative scores.

C02 reports maximal target_alignment, verifier_alignment, and quality_control (all 1.0), whereas C01 reports zero alignment. Given the evaluation metric dr_cate_lift favors higher target alignment, C02 is expected to yield higher downstream utility.
C02 shows higher feedback_locality and quality_control while matching C01 on retention_control, source_diversity, and target_alignment, suggesting higher expected accuracy in the finance domain.
C02 has higher feedback locality and quality control while retention control, source diversity, and target alignment are equal, indicating a higher expected accuracy in the finance domain.

Finance panels show that broader or more diverse data (synthetic sources, farthest selections) often improve accuracy. The target candidates differ in threshold range width and sample size; broader ranges and larger sample counts (C01) are expected to yield higher downstream utility, followed by the next widest and most data-rich candidates (C03, C05), with the narrower, lower-sample candidates (C02, C04) ranked lower.

The finance panels show higher accuracy when training data is more diverse (synthetic or farthest selections). Candidates with larger sample counts and broader difficulty thresholds (e.g., C01 with 0.1‑0.9 and 7310 samples) are therefore expected to yield higher downstream utility. C03 balances a moderate range (0.2‑0.8) with a sizable sample set, C05 has a similar range but a slightly narrower lower bound, C02 excludes the hardest examples (upper bound 0.7) and has fewer samples, and C04 has the smallest sample count and narrowest range, leading to the lowest expected utility.

The target_alignment values (0.0–1.0) directly indicate predicted alignment with the accuracy metric; higher values imply higher expected downstream utility, so candidates are ranked descending by these values.

Finance panels measuring accuracy_percent show that higher quality_control and verifier_alignment values consistently yield higher observed utilities. C01 has full scores (1.0) on these measures, while C02‑C04 have intermediate scores (0.667), leading to an estimated normalized utility of ~0.69 versus 1.0 for C01.

All candidates share identical measurement values except verifier_alignment; C03 has the highest alignment (1), C04 moderate (0.5), C01 low (0.25), and C02 none (0). Since the target is an RL finance task, the presence of an RL stage (absent for C02) further favors C01‑C04. Thus we rank C03 > C04 > C01 > C02.

All candidates include an SFT stage, but only the chain‑of‑thought variants (C01, C03) provide reasoning‑oriented data, which is valuable for finance tasks. C03 uses a high quality‑control level (1) despite a smaller data fraction (0.6), likely yielding more reliable outputs than C01’s larger data fraction (1) with lower quality control (0.7). The original QA variant (C04) lacks quality control and relies on raw volume only, giving moderate expected utility. The base model (C02) has no training signals, so it is expected to perform worst.

The zero‑shot force MAE values (lower is better) serve as a proxy for model quality; better model quality is expected to translate into higher downstream utility under the higher‑is‑better panel_normalized_joint_utility metric. Hence the candidate with the lowest MAE (C03) is ranked highest, followed by C01, then C02.

The only available data are zero‑shot force prediction MAE values; lower MAE generally indicates more accurate predictions, which in materials‑science workflows translates to higher downstream utility. Using the inverse of MAE as a proxy and normalising, C01 (0.086 eV/Å) > C02 (0.109 eV/Å) > C03 (0.319 eV/Å). The mapping from MAE to the target panel_normalized_joint_utility is not explicit, so confidence is moderate.

Panels for energy RMSE show that the energy‑focused 'Leverage' intervention outperforms the force‑focused 'Block Leverage'. The two target candidates differ only in trajectory stride: C02 samples a longer trajectory (10× relative span) with a coarser stride, analogous to the energy‑focused approach, while C01 samples a shorter trajectory with finer stride, analogous to the force‑focused approach. Therefore C02 is expected to yield higher native utility. Confidence moderate due to indirect mapping.

The panels contain no direct measurements of trajectory stride or relative span, and both candidates share identical training configuration counts and pretrained initialization. Without evidence linking these differences to utility, we cannot meaningfully order them, so we abstain from a confident ranking.

Finance panels show that interventions with source_diversity=2 (financial cpt plus sft) outperformed those with source_diversity=1 (synthetic finance sft) in 3 of 4 comparisons, indicating higher expected accuracy for the candidate with matching source_diversity (C01). The remaining candidates all have source_diversity=1 and no direct evidence differentiates them, so they receive similar lower scores. Confidence is moderate due to limited data for the real-data candidate (C05).

Finance panels show that interventions using convfinqa (a non‑finqa data source) consistently achieve higher accuracy than those using only finqa data. This pattern suggests that synthetic‑like finqa data may provide higher downstream utility than real finqa data for the target environment, though the evidence is indirect and does not involve the exact synthetic data of C02, leading to moderate confidence.

C01 has the target density inside its training range, the smallest density gap (0.3 g/cm³) and a large density span (0.7 g/cm³), aligning with the decision context that emphasizes density diversity. C02 and C03 both lack density diversity and have the target density outside their training range; C03 includes a temperature span (200 K) whereas C02 has none, giving C03 a modest advantage. Consequently, the expected downstream utility ranking is C01 > C03 > C02.

C01 exactly matches the target density (gap 0) and its training data includes a substantial density span, directly supporting the density‑diversity goal; C03 lacks density diversity but provides temperature diversity, offering modest relevance; C02 has neither density nor temperature variation, making it the least likely to yield high utility.

C01 exactly matches the target temperature (1000 K) and has zero high‑energy count gap, indicating the closest alignment to the target environment and thus the highest expected utility. C03 is moderately close in temperature (600 K, 400 K gap) and high‑energy count gap, giving it the next highest utility. C04 has a large temperature gap (350 K, 650 K gap) and does not match the target's uncertainty bias (uncertainty_bias_matches_target=0, uses_uncertainty_bias=1), lowering its expected utility. C02 is farthest from the target in both temperature and high‑energy count, leading to the lowest expected utility.

C02 has zero high‑energy count gap and zero temperature gap to the target and matches the target's uncertainty bias, giving it the highest expected native utility. C03 is moderately close on both high‑energy and temperature gaps and also matches the bias, placing it next. C04 matches the temperature gap but does not match the uncertainty bias and uses uncertainty bias, reducing its expected utility relative to C03. C01 is far from the target on both high‑energy and temperature gaps and has a large temperature deviation, resulting in the lowest expected utility.

C01 (QBC) employs committee disagreement and model‑relative signal, active‑learning heuristics that generally improve sample efficiency and downstream utility compared with random selection, which uses none of these cues. No direct experimental panels are available, so the ordering is based on these methodological differences, yielding moderate confidence.

In the retrieved materials‑science panels, QBC consistently outperformed random but was inferior to model‑disagreement/uncertainty methods (e.g., ts disagreement, nsga disagreement) that achieved near‑optimal utilities. The target task uses a random‑forest model (mp rf), so an acquisition that queries the same model’s uncertainty (rfMaxUncertainty) is expected to be most effective, with xgbMaxUncertainty also strong but slightly less aligned. Random acquisition is expected to be the worst.

C03 combines a very high DFT fraction, uses model-relative uncertainty partition, and has the lowest uncertainty cutoff, giving it the highest expected utility. C02 has full DFT data but lacks model-relative partitioning, placing it second. C05, despite low DFT content, matches an independently validated uncertainty cutoff and uses model-relative partitioning, yielding moderate utility. C04 balances DFT and UMLIP with a moderate cutoff, giving slightly lower utility than C05. C06 has low DFT and a very high uncertainty cutoff, reducing its utility. C01 contains only UMLIP data, no model-relative partition, and no uncertainty cutoff, resulting in the lowest expected utility.

Higher DFT fractions improve force accuracy, while use of relative uncertainty partition and moderate uncertainty cutoffs enhance UQ calibration. C03 (95% DFT, relative partition, low cutoff) is expected to give the best utility, followed by C04 (balanced DFT/UMLIP mix, relative partition, moderate cutoff). C05, despite low DFT, meets an independent validation threshold, giving moderate utility. C02 has full DFT but lacks uncertainty partition and cutoff, reducing UQ performance. C06 and C01 have low DFT fractions and poor UQ settings, leading to lower expected utility.

C01 has the highest effective signal coverage (0.73) and very high chemical system entropy, indicating broad, representative training data that should lower phonon MAE. C04 offers moderate coverage (0.43) with a larger number of chemical systems, giving it the next best expected utility despite lower signal density. C02 and C03 both have low coverage (<0.14) even though they have high signal density; limited coverage likely leads to poorer generalization and higher MAE, with C02 slightly ahead of C03 due to marginally higher entropy and coverage.

Base (C01) matches the 'base' interventions in finance panels, which show low to moderate normalized utilities (0.0–0.53). Distilled cot (C02) aligns with 'self distilled sft' and 'filtered cot' that consistently achieve the highest normalized utility (≈1.0). Partial cot (C03) is intermediate between full cot (≈0.65) and filtered cot (≈1.0), suggesting a moderate utility (~0.7). Raw data (C04) mirrors 'original qa' and 'ordinary sft' that score near zero, indicating very low utility.

Each target candidate was compared to finance‑domain panel interventions using Euclidean distance on the prediction‑time measurement vectors. Inverse‑distance weighting of the observed within‑panel normalized utilities yielded expected utilities: distilled cot (C02) aligns with top‑performing filtered‑cot and self‑distilled SFT, giving the highest score; distilled plus table calculation (C04) is close to filtered‑cot and self‑distilled SFT, yielding a high but slightly lower score; partial cot (C05) matches filtered‑SFT and filtered‑cot, giving a moderate score; distilled plus general math (C03) includes out‑of‑domain data, reducing similarity to finance‑specific interventions and lowering its score; the base model (C01) matches low‑utility baselines, resulting in a low score; raw data (C06) matches the worst‑performing raw‑volume candidates, giving near‑zero utility.

Both candidates have identical quality_control (1.0) and target_alignment (1.0). C01 has higher source_diversity (2 vs 1), which is likely to improve model generalization in the finance domain, leading to higher expected accuracy.

Both candidates have equal quality_control (1.0) and target_alignment (1.0). C01 shows higher source_diversity (2 vs 1), which is likely to provide broader training data and improve accuracy for finance tasks, suggesting higher expected downstream utility for C01.

C01 contains the full convfinqa dataset, directly matching the target environment's focus, so it is expected to yield the highest accuracy. C02 mixes finqa and convfinqa with one‑third convfinqa data, giving moderate expected utility. C04 and C03 have no convfinqa data; however, C04's larger finqa sample size may provide a slight advantage over C03.

C04 contains full tatqa data (target_fraction=1.0) directly matching the tatqa task, giving the highest expected accuracy. C01 mixes finqa and tatqa (target_fraction≈0.33) providing moderate relevance. C03 and C02 are finqa‑only (target_fraction=0) and thus less aligned; C03’s larger sample size gives it a slight edge over C02.

C04 has the highest proportion of 'better' outcomes (0.593), the lowest demonstration steps, and a moderate Cupid rank, indicating the highest expected closed‑loop success. C02 and C03 have higher Cupid rank percentiles but lower 'better' proportions and longer steps, placing them next. C01 is balanced across tiers with moderate steps. C05 shows the lowest 'better' proportion and longest steps, suggesting the lowest expected utility.

Random selection (C03) consistently received a normalized utility of 0.0 in both robotics panels, indicating the lowest expected downstream utility. Diversity‑focused selections (e.g., cupid tier balanced, cupid 50) achieved high utilities (~0.72‑0.76), supporting a high expected utility for the diversity‑only candidate (C02). Coverage‑type selections (e.g., coverage 50, failure coverage) showed moderate utilities (~0.46‑0.48), suggesting a middle expected utility for the calibration‑retain candidate (C01). Mapping these patterns yields the ranking C02 > C01 > C03.

The retrieved robotics panel reports closed-loop success rates for 'all data', 'length 50', and 'random 50', which match target candidates C01, C05, and C06, yielding normalized utilities of 0.76, 1.0, and 0.0 respectively. No panel provides outcomes for the interventions described as 'coverage 50', 'failure coverage 50', or 'failure coverage short 50', so we lack direct evidence for C02‑C04. To avoid inferring outcomes from possible aliasing, we assign those candidates a neutral placeholder score. Because two candidates have no evidence, we set abstain to true and confidence low.

C03 allocates training uniformly across all task categories, which best matches the equal-task macro completion metric; C02 has moderately balanced but still non‑uniform weights; C01’s weights are more skewed toward a subset of tasks, likely reducing macro‑averaged performance despite its selection rule.

C02 has perfect target distribution match (1.0) while C01 has none (0), which is critical for downstream performance; although C01 shows higher structural coverage, the lack of distribution alignment likely reduces its utility, so C02 is expected to achieve higher native utility.

C02 has perfect target distribution match (1) while C01 has none (0). Although C01 shows higher structural coverage (0.996 vs 0.642), the perfect distribution match of C02 is more predictive of downstream utility in the materials‑science context, leading to higher expected utility for C02.

The ranking is based on the provided prediction_time_measurements. Higher data_fraction (more supervised fine‑tuning data) is expected to improve QuantEval knowledge accuracy, and the presence of RL_stage and verifier_alignment (both set to 1 for C03) further suggests better factual performance. C01 has no fine‑tuning data, while C04 and C05 use only 25% and 50% of the data respectively, leading to lower expected utility.

Ranking uses the provided prediction_time_measurements: higher data_fraction, presence of RL stage, verifier alignment, and SFT stage are associated with higher expected QuantEval reasoning accuracy, leading to C03 > C02 > C05 > C04 > C01.

C03 has the highest sum of prediction-time measurements (including verifier_alignment=1), C02 matches C03 on all other metrics but lacks verifier_alignment, and C01 scores zero on all measurements, indicating the lowest expected downstream utility.

C03 has the highest values for quality_control, retention_control, source_diversity, and target_alignment, indicating the strongest expected downstream utility for finance accuracy; C02 follows with strong quality_control and target_alignment but no retention_control; C04 has target_alignment but lacks quality and retention control; C01 shows no positive measurements.

Finance panels show that a plain 'base' model achieved ~69% accuracy (norm. utility 0.69) while a plain SFT model performed poorly (0% utility). The 'fin sd' method (localized self‑distillation) reached the highest utility (1.0) and 'opsd' was intermediate (0.82). C01 matches the plain base condition, C02 matches plain SFT, C04 adds QA refinement which resembles the fin‑sd approach and is expected to be near the top, C05 combines both QA and transcript refinements and is expected to be the best, while C03 adds only transcript refinement and is expected to improve over plain SFT but remain below the base level.

C01 (base) directly matches the 'base' intervention in the finance panel with a within‑panel normalized utility of ~0.69. C02 (plain SFT) matches the 'sft' intervention, which had the lowest utility (0.0). Adding transcript refinement (C03) is analogous to using synthetic data (panel 3) that modestly improved accuracy, suggesting a moderate uplift (~0.75). Adding QA refinement (C04) resembles the farthest‑selection data strategy (panel 4) that achieved the highest utility, indicating a higher uplift (~0.80). Combining both refinements (C05) aligns with the best‑performing self‑distillation and synthetic‑data methods (fin‑sd, synthetic) that reached normalized utility 1.0, so we assign it the highest expected utility (~0.95).

Materials‑science panels show QBC‑style methods (committee disagreement + model‑relative signal) usually outperform random, though one panel shows the opposite, indicating variability. Robotics panels demonstrate that diversity‑aware acquisition improves over random, supporting the value of LCMD‑based methods. The target decision context explicitly mentions a "force aware NTK" setting, so candidates that incorporate NTK (parameter‑derivative) and force signals (C05, C06) are expected to deliver the highest native utility, with NTK‑only (C04) next. Committee‑based candidates (C02, C03) are beneficial but less aligned with the force‑aware NTK focus, placing them after the NTK group. The activation candidate (C01) benefits from diversity‑aware LCMD, ranking above random (C07), which serves as the baseline.

In three of four materials‑science panels, QBC (which uses committee disagreement) achieved higher native utility than random, indicating that committee‑based acquisition methods are likely to outperform random. Robotics panels show that diversity‑aware selection (similar to the LCMD feature) outperforms random, suggesting a benefit from diversity‑aware LCMD. The target context stresses a force‑aware NTK model, so candidates that include force signals and NTK (C05, C06) or force alone (C03) are expected to be advantageous despite lacking direct evidence. Activation (C01) lacks both committee disagreement and NTK, and random (C07) is the baseline. These considerations lead to the ranking C03 > C02 > C05 > C06 > C04 > C01 > C07.

C01 employs dataset entropy, adaptive acquisition, target‑distribution matching, and structural‑coverage selection, all of which directly support the target environment's emphasis on entropy‑driven carbon distribution. C02 lacks these mechanisms and is purely random, suggesting a lower expected native utility.

C01 employs dataset entropy, structural coverage selection, adaptive acquisition, and matches the target distribution, which directly aligns with the decision context emphasizing dataset-aware entropy for silicon; C02 lacks these features, suggesting lower expected downstream utility.

C02 exhibits lower energy MAE/RMSE and lower effective coverage errors, which are primary drivers of native utility in materials‑science models. While C01 has slightly better force error density, p90, and vector RMSE, the differences are modest compared to C02's substantial improvements in energy and coverage metrics, leading to an expectation of higher downstream utility for C02.

C02 exhibits substantially lower energy MAE/RMSE and lower effective coverage errors, which are primary drivers of native utility in materials‑science predictions. C01 only marginally improves force‑related metrics, so the overall expected downstream utility is higher for C02.
